titulo: Australian Minister for Energy lowers fuel standards for 60 days amid rising oil prices, panic buying

fuente.nota: Text shortened by removing paragraphs; the sentences are unchanged.

parrafos: Chris Bowen, Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, allowed the usage of dirtier fuel with elevated sulfur content for 60 days, he announced on Thursday. As a part of the change, the oil refineries were required to prioritise supply to farmers in rural areas. This decision followed issues with oil exports caused by the ongoing Middle East conflict, as fuel prices rose rapidly to over A$2/L.

The lower quality oil was previously exported to countries with lower fuel standards. With the new temporarily changes in place, it would now be allowed to be used in Australia. One of the two oil refineries, Ampol, noted rural areas supply would be prioritised.
Additionally, Bowen announced Australia would release 100 million liters from its reserve oil supply per month, in response to a request from the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The issue appeared related to the growing demand while supply was essentially unchanged. As people stockpiled fuel, and the demand has doubled, there were concerns over panic buying by Australians. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese commented on longer term impacts of the situation on economics in Australia, talking with ABC Television on Thursday.

President of the National Farmer Federation commented noting the government regulation was direly needed in this situation as farmers and fishers were struggling to access fuel, especially in remote areas. He also noted that government should prepare strategies in case the situation 'deteriorates', mentioning access to diesel was a pre-requisite for the farmers running the agricultural areas, collecting crops, transporting crops, and providing food to the country.

In reserve, Australia had 36 days worth of petrol, 32 days worth of diesel, and 29 days worth of jet fuel, respectively. These fell short of the 90 days requirement under obligations for the IEA, of which Australia is a member. Opposition was calling on the government to ensure fuel security, ABC News reported.
titulo_es: Australian Energy Minister relaxes fuel standards for 60 days in response to rising oil prices and panic buying
resumen_es: Australia temporarily allows fuel with a higher sulphur content, prioritises supply to farmers and releases oil reserves in response to the price rises caused by the conflict in the Middle East and consumer stockpiling.

ideas_clave.idea: Australia's energy minister temporarily authorised lower-quality, high-sulfur fuel for 60 days, previously sent abroad, and asked refineries to give priority to rural farmers.
The measure responds to export disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict, which pushed fuel prices above two Australian dollars per litre.
At the request of the IEA, the country will also release 100 million litres a month from its reserves, as stockpiling has doubled demand while supply has stayed flat.
Farmers' representatives welcomed the decision, stressing that diesel is essential for food production and calling for contingency plans if the situation worsens.
Australia's fuel reserves cover only about a month, well below the 90 days required by the IEA, and the opposition is demanding guarantees of fuel security.

resumen_modelo: The article reports that Australia's energy minister, Chris Bowen, has relaxed fuel standards for 60 days, allowing high-sulfur fuel previously exported to be used domestically. This response to the Middle East conflict, which has pushed prices above two Australian dollars per litre, also obliges refineries to prioritise rural farmers, for whom diesel is vital. Moreover, at the IEA's request, the government will release monthly reserves, while panic buying has doubled demand. Nevertheless, national stocks fall well short of the 90 days the IEA requires, prompting opposition calls for greater fuel security.
